trial_name: WATERFALL — Aggressive or Moderate Fluid Resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis (2022)
citation: de-Madaria E, Buxbaum JL, Maisonneuve P, et al. Aggressive or moderate fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(11):989-1000.
one_liner: Aggressive fluid resuscitation did not reduce severity of acute pancreatitis but increased fluid overload, supporting a moderate, reassessment-driven strategy.

pico.population: Adults ≥18 years with acute pancreatitis diagnosed within 8 hours, symptom onset within 24 hours, no baseline organ failure or high-risk comorbidities (decompensated heart failure, chronic renal failure).
pico.intervention: Aggressive lactated Ringer's: 20 mL/kg bolus over 2 hours, then 3 mL/kg/h infusion, with protocolised reassessment at 3, 12, 24, 48, 72 hours and adjustment/cessation per clinical targets.
pico.comparison: Moderate lactated Ringer's: 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h infusion, with identical reassessment and adjustment rules.
pico.outcome: Primary: moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis (composite severity endpoint during index admission). Key safety: fluid overload.

background.existing_knowledge: Early IV crystalloid is standard supportive care for acute pancreatitis to mitigate hypovolaemia. Guidelines historically recommended early aggressive hydration based on physiology and observational data.
background.knowledge_gap: Evidence for aggressive hydration was weak, and there was concern about iatrogenic fluid overload causing respiratory compromise.
background.hypothesis: Early aggressive, weight-based lactated Ringer's resuscitation would reduce moderately severe or severe pancreatitis compared with a moderate, reassessment-guided strategy, without increasing harm.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, open-label, parallel-group, investigator-initiated superiority trial; ED-based enrolment across 18 centres in four countries (India, Italy, Mexico, Spain); enrolment May 2020 to September 2021.

inclusion: Acute pancreatitis diagnosed using standard criteria
Diagnosis within 8 hours prior to randomisation
exclusion: Pancreatitis severity already declaring itself (baseline organ failure)
Other conditions at high risk of fluid complications or requiring alternative resuscitation strategies

methods.intervention: Aggressive lactated Ringer's: 20 mL/kg bolus over 2 hours followed by 3 mL/kg/hour infusion. Reassessment checkpoints (3, 12, 24, 48, 72 hours): infusion adjusted per protocolised clinical targets (including signs of hypovolaemia/overload) and stopped/reduced as oral intake resumed. Fluid overload management: mandated reduction/cessation of infusion, with diuretics and supportive therapies at clinician discretion when overload criteria met.
methods.comparison: Moderate lactated Ringer's: 10 mL/kg bolus over 2 hours only if baseline hypovolaemia present; otherwise no initial bolus. Maintenance 1.5 mL/kg/hour with the same scheduled reassessment and protocolised adjustment/cessation rules as the intervention arm. Rescue/co-interventions: additional therapies (imaging, nutrition, antibiotics, procedures) per treating teams; protocol focused on fluid strategy rather than downstream management algorithms.
methods.blinding: Open-label (fluid rates/boluses not feasibly blinded); raises risk of performance bias for discretionary outcomes, but primary and many key components were clinically anchored and protocol-defined.
methods.sample_size_power: A total sample size of 744 patients was planned to detect a 10% absolute difference in the primary outcome (35% vs 25%) with 80% power at a two-sided 5% significance level, incorporating O'Brien–Fleming interim monitoring and an allowance for attrition, with a modified intention-to-treat primary analysis.
methods.primary_outcome: Moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis (composite severity endpoint during index admission)
secondary_outcomes: Composite of death, persistent organ failure, or infected necrotising pancreatitis
methods.follow_up: Protocolised clinical reassessments through 72 hours; primary and major secondary outcomes assessed during the index hospitalisation.

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early after first interim analysis (n=249) due to excess fluid overload without benefit.
Primary outcome not improved: moderately severe/severe pancreatitis 22.1% vs 17.3% (adjusted RR 1.30, 95% CI 0.78–2.18, p=0.32).
Fluid overload significantly increased: 20.5% vs 6.3% (adjusted RR 2.85, 95% CI 1.36–5.94, p=0.004).
Median fluid volume 0–12h: 3.7 L vs 2.0 L; 0–72h: 8.3 L vs 6.6 L.
Early termination limits precision for efficacy and low-frequency endpoints.

outcomes_table.outcome: Moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis (primary)
outcomes_table.note: Composite severity endpoint during index admission
Organ failure by modified Marshall criteria

outcomes_table.outcome: Death, persistent organ failure, or infected necrotising pancreatitis

outcomes_table.note: Longer stay consistent with higher overload/respiratory complications

safety: Fluid overload occurred in 20.5% vs 6.3% (adjusted RR 2.85, p=0.004).
Diuretic use and oxygen supplementation were more frequent in the aggressive arm.

domains.notes: Central randomisation with stratification (centre; baseline SIRS; baseline hypovolaemia) and concealed allocation via electronic system; reduces selection bias.
Open-label design may influence discretionary care (e.g., discharge decisions), but core outcomes (organ failure, death, ICU admission) are relatively objective and protocol-defined.
All 249 randomised included in reported comparison; missing outcome data minimal for primary and most clinical endpoints.

Protocol mandated scheduled reassessment at 3, 12, 24, 48, 72 hours with prespecified rate adjustments; fluid overload triggered reduction/cessation and diuretic use, likely attenuating ongoing exposure in aggressive arm after harm emerged. Clear early fluid separation: 0–12h median 3.7 L vs 2.0 L; 0–72h 8.3 L vs 6.6 L.
Generally balanced in age (54.7 vs 56.4 years) and BMI (26.8 vs 26.3 kg/m²); modest sex imbalance (men 44.3% vs 53.5%); aetiology similar (biliary 54.1% vs 54.3%; alcoholic 23.0% vs 21.3%).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate. Allocation methods and protocolisation were strong, and the harm signal is internally credible; however, open-label care and early termination materially limit the precision of efficacy and many secondary outcome estimates.

domains.notes: Patients enrolled early in the ED, largely with mild disease at baseline (no baseline organ failure), reflecting a common clinical entry point, but excluding many high-risk patients (cardiac/renal comorbidity; established organ failure) who often complicate real-world fluid decisions. Aetiology predominantly biliary and alcohol-related; applicability to hypertriglyceridaemia, post-ERCP, or complex iatrogenic cases less certain.

Conducted across four countries with heterogeneous ward/ICU thresholds; biological harm mechanism (volume-related pulmonary congestion) should generalise. Findings most directly inform early ED/ward management of uncomplicated acute pancreatitis; extrapolation to patients in shock, with evolving organ failure, or requiring ICU-level resuscitation should be cautious and individualized.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate. Results are highly relevant to early ED-presenting acute pancreatitis without established organ failure, but are less generalisable to older, multimorbid patients and those with early severe physiology where aggressive resuscitation may be unavoidable.

strengths: Pragmatic ED enrolment in the early window
Prespecified interim monitoring with DSMB oversight
limitations: Open-label (risk of performance bias for discretionary outcomes)
Composite primary outcome may complicate mechanistic interpretation
Exclusions limit generalisability to high-risk cardiopulmonary/renal populations

critical_appraisal.summary: WATERFALL is a well-designed, pragmatic RCT that provides moderate-quality evidence against routine aggressive fluid resuscitation in early acute pancreatitis. The harm signal (fluid overload) is robust, but early termination and open-label design limit confidence in efficacy estimates.
strengths: Pragmatic ED enrolment in the early window
weaknesses: Open-label (risk of performance bias for discretionary outcomes)
Composite primary outcome may complicate mechanistic interpretation
Exclusions limit generalisability to high-risk cardiopulmonary/renal populations

sections.authors_conclusion: Aggressive LR strategy did not reduce moderately severe/severe pancreatitis but substantially increased fluid overload, shifting the risk–benefit balance against routine aggressive hydration. A default approach of moderate maintenance (~1.5 mL/kg/h) with boluses reserved for demonstrable hypovolaemia is better aligned with safety.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not use routine aggressive fluid resuscitation in early acute pancreatitis; use moderate maintenance with bolus only for hypovolaemia, and reassess frequently.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with acute pancreatitis presenting to the ED within 24 hours of symptom onset, without baseline organ failure or significant cardiopulmonary/renal comorbidities.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not mean that all fluid should be withheld; patients with hypovolaemia still require boluses, and those with shock or organ failure may need individualized resuscitation.
implementation_caveats: Frequent reassessment (at 3, 12, 24, 48, 72 hours) is essential to adjust fluid rates and detect overload early.
Lactated Ringer's is the preferred crystalloid.
Avoid automatic high-rate infusions; de-escalate as oral intake resumes.

controversies.notes: The DSMB-driven halt strengthens confidence in the safety signal but makes efficacy estimates imprecise; the absence of benefit cannot be interpreted as definitive equivalence.

The primary endpoint aggregates different severity constructs (local complications, systemic complications, organ failure, comorbidity exacerbation), which can dilute mechanistic specificity even when clinically meaningful.

Discretionary endpoints (hospital length of stay) could be influenced by clinician awareness of assignment; however, imaging use was similar and objective outcomes (fluid overload criteria, organ failure, death) anchor the main message.

Contemporary commentary emphasised that WATERFALL provides high-quality evidence against routine aggressive hydration and highlighted the practical message: bolus for hypovolaemia only, and reassess frequently to avoid pulmonary congestion.

Post-WATERFALL meta-analyses focusing on RCT evidence generally report no improvement in clinically important outcomes with aggressive strategies but increased fluid overload/respiratory complications, reinforcing the trial's harm signal.

Newer guidance increasingly favours more conservative, goal-directed fluid with lactated Ringer's and explicit avoidance of indiscriminate 'aggressive' resuscitation, reflecting incorporation of WATERFALL's safety findings into recommendations.

unresolved_questions: Optimal fluid strategy in patients with baseline organ failure or shock remains uncertain.
Long-term outcomes beyond index hospitalization not assessed.
Role of balanced crystalloids other than LR not studied.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In early acute pancreatitis, aggressive fluid resuscitation increases fluid overload without improving severity; use moderate maintenance and bolus only for hypovolaemia.
